title: Who kills newborns, and does it explain why viscosity protects populations?
question: Q found (not pre-registered) that populations whose newborns were placed beside a non-relative went extinct in 11/12 runs, against 3/12 when newborns were placed beside their parent. Is that because non-relatives kill newborns? This study logs every killing in the first 6000 ticks: whether the killer is a relative, whether it is the victim's parent, and whether the victim is young (age < 150 ticks).
background: A pilot on unregistered seed 9997 (3000 ticks, one run per placement) leaned against the stranger-attack idea: 62% (stranger) and 74% (viscous) of kills hit young agents, who made up 33% and 28% of agent-ticks; 59% of kills in the viscous run were of relatives. H31b is the mechanism Q suggested and is registered in that direction even though the pilot does not favour it. early_young_kill_excess = share of kills with a young victim minus the share of agent-ticks spent young. Seeds 1600-1611 have never been run.

hypotheses.statement: Young agents are killed more often than their share of the population (viscous)
Young agents are killed more often than their share of the population (stranger)
Newborns placed beside a stranger are killed more (excess young kills higher than when placed beside the parent)
Replication of Q (post hoc there): populations whose newborns sit beside a stranger die out sooner than viscous ones
In viscous populations, parents kill their own offspring in at least 10% of killings
